To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a territorial cohesion strategy for Europe should be developed, which should be based upon a common understanding of the meaning of territorial cohesion, a common vision of the future of European territories, and a common set of principles of good territorial governance in the EU; (b) the territorial cohesion strategy should be developed by means of a European territorial planning process, which should be coordinated at the national level, but which should also be based upon the principles of vertical and horizontal subsidiarity, as well as

(1) the new Constitution, in its Article III-402, recognizes the importance of territorial cohesion; (2) this recognition should be translated into a new planning policy for the EU; and (3) such a new planning policy should be grounded on the principles of vertical subsidiarity, of horizontal subsidiarity, of the coordination between subsidiary and cohesion, and of the coordination of the planning systems in the Member States.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the principles of subsidiarity and territorial cohesion.
the relationship between territorial cohesion and the principle of subsidiarity, and how the principle of subsidiary coordination might be applied to the planning system.
how the principles of subsidiarity and cohesion are being applied in the EU and the implications of this for the future development of the planning system in the EU.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the EU is not a unitary state and that it should be governed by a system of subsidiarity and cohesion, not by the pursuit of territorial coherence and the principle of solidarity, the latter of which would lead to the establishment of a central planning authority at the EU level.
subsidiarity and territorial cohesion should be considered as two complementary principles of good territorial governance, and that the new European Constitution should be amended to this end.

the Constitution should be interpreted as a call for a new form of governance in which the EU and national levels of government are not in competition with each other but rather are in a relationship of mutual cooperation and coordination.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the European Union should become a more effective actor in territorial governance, and that this should be based on the principle of subsidiarity.
the new European Constitution should at least provide a basis for a discussion about principles of good territorial governance in the common area.

the EU should not be the only one responsible for territorial cohesion, but rather that the EU should encourage national governments, regional and local administrations to take the initiative in this field.
The main takeaway from our work is that
territorial cohesion and subsidiarity should not be seen as mutually exclusive.

the EU should not try to replace national systems of territorial governance but rather encourage the development of a European territorial governance framework that would support the coordination of national planning processes.
, in a context of increasing territorial complexity and diversity, subsidiarity is not a mere principle of devolution of power, but a principle of good territorial governance.
